issues.legal_issue: A court may reconsider an earlier direction in pending public-interest litigation when the earlier consideration omitted a material statutory impact and the controversy concerns grave public importance.
material_facts: The earlier direction allowed some mines to operate without addressing the effect of the forest-conservation legislation already in force.
The proceedings had not been finally disposed of, and the earlier direction had exempted certain mines from further scrutiny rather than releasing them from the proceedings.
The litigation concerned the environmental and social consequences of mining, and leaving the issue open risked multiplicity of proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The earlier direction did not prevent the Court from reconsidering the mines, and the Court could decide the issue in the pending proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: In public-interest litigation, procedural rules apply, but procedural technicalities are not always available as a defence when grave public importance is at stake. The Court stated that even if an earlier order were treated as final, it would be difficult to apply res judicata in a dispute of this type, particularly where relevant statutory impact had not been considered.

predicates.public_interest_writ: The proceeding is a public-interest writ concerning environmental conditions rather than an ordinary dispute between private parties.
predicates.grave_public_importance: The issue concerns safety, environmental conditions, or other interests of substantial importance to the public.
predicates.earlier_direction_omitted_material_statu: An earlier direction was made without considering the impact of a material legal requirement already in force.

issues.definition: When a public-interest writ raises a matter of grave public importance and an earlier direction omitted a material legal impact, the Court may reconsider that direction.

issues.legal_issue: The existence of a later statutory environmental process does not require a court to decline jurisdiction over a public-interest proceeding already substantially heard and considered.
material_facts: The writ proceedings began more than three years before the environmental-protection statute came into force.
The Court had appointed expert committees, received reports, issued directions, and heard the parties at length before the statute came into force.
The statute empowered the Central Government to take measures to protect and improve the environment but did not purport to remove the Court’s jurisdiction over this proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The Court was not required to decline jurisdiction in favour of authorities under the later statute and could continue to decide the pending case.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinarily, a court may decline to entertain a dispute for which a special statutory procedure exists, but that is a rule of practice and prudence, not jurisdiction. The later environmental statute did not take away the Court’s jurisdiction over this case.

predicates.public_interest_writ: The proceeding is a public-interest writ concerning environmental protection.
predicates.proceeding_precedes_later_environmental_: The proceeding began before a later statute created an environmental-protection process.
predicates.court_has_substantially_heard_case: The Court has received expert reports, issued directions, and heard the parties substantially before considering whether to decline jurisdiction.

issues.definition: A court may continue hearing a public-interest environmental proceeding begun before a later environmental process when it has already substantially considered the case.

issues.legal_issue: The forest-conservation requirements apply to grants and renewals of mining leases in forest land, and a renewal option does not dispense with the required prior approval.
material_facts: Most of the mines were in reserved forests or other forest land.
Some lessees sought renewals after their leases expired, including lessees relying on an option to renew in their lease agreements.
The required prior approval of the Central Government had not been obtained for the renewals at issue.
issues.conclusion: The forest-conservation statute applied to renewals as well as first grants, and prior approval was a condition precedent to renewal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 requires prior approval of the Central Government before forest land is used for a non-forest purpose. The Court held that this requirement applies to renewal of mining leases, including renewal sought under an option in a lease. It relied on Ambica Quarry Works v. State of Gujarat, [1987] 1 SCC 213, and distinguished State of Bihar v. Banshi Ram Modi, [1985] 3 SCC 643; it also stated that State of Rajasthan v. Hari Shankar Rajindra Pal, [1965] 3 SCR 402 did not apply to the facts.

rule.if: mining_lease_in_forest_land and grant_or_renewal_sought and not prior_central_approval_obtained

predicates.mining_lease_in_forest_land: The mining lease concerns land that is forest land.
predicates.grant_or_renewal_sought: A party seeks a first grant or renewal of the mining lease.
predicates.prior_central_approval_obtained: The required prior approval of the Central Government has been obtained for the non-forest use of the land.

issues.definition: A grant or renewal sought for mining in forest land cannot be validly made when the required prior approval has not been obtained.

issues.legal_issue: Mining in a forested area that is harmed by mining cannot continue as a permanent activity, although closure may be phased to allow adjustment and existing valid leases may run to their original expiry subject to safeguards.
material_facts: Expert committees reported environmental damage from mining, including forest damage, debris and scree, blocked or reduced water flows, and harm to ecological balance.
The Court found that mining adversely affected the environment and conservation of forests, and that the area was substantially forest land.
The Union Government reported that limestone of the required quality was available from other indigenous sources, though those sources could not immediately replace existing supply.
The Court found that an abrupt stop would harm industries and accepted a limited continuation for three mines operating under unexpired original leases, subject to conditions.
issues.conclusion: Mining in the area had to be totally stopped as a continuing activity, but the transition was to be phased; the three ongoing mines with unexpired original leases could continue only until their lease terms ended and subject to safeguards.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, the constitutional recognition of environmental protection in Articles 48A and 51A(g), and the evidence of environmental harm. It held that preservation of forests and ecological balance took precedence over continued exploitation, while allowing a transition rather than an abrupt closure because of the practical effects on industry.

predicates.public_interest_writ: The proceeding is a public-interest writ addressing the environmental consequences of mining.
predicates.mining_adversely_affects_ecology: Evidence in the case shows that mining harms ecological balance or the environment.
predicates.mining_area_is_forest_land: The mining area is forest land or is substantially covered by forest.

issues.definition: Where a public-interest environmental proceeding establishes ecological harm from mining in forest land, mining must end after any transition the Court permits.

issues.legal_issue: Court orders or decrees enabling continued mining or renewal cannot preserve a lease where the required forest-conservation approval was absent.
material_facts: Several leases had expired and renewal requests had been refused.
The lessees continued mining under orders or decrees obtained from different courts.
The forest-conservation approval required for renewal had not been obtained, and all affected parties had been heard in the proceedings.
issues.conclusion: Orders and decrees relating to renewal without the required approval were to stand vacated, and related appeals or proceedings to obtain renewal or challenge renewal decisions were to become ineffective.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 makes prior approval a condition precedent to use of forest land for a non-forest purpose, including renewal of a mining lease. Relying on Ambica Quarry Works v. State of Gujarat, [1987] 1 SCC 213, the Court held that an order made in disregard of that requirement would not bind and could be nullified. The Court also found that nullifying the orders in the circumstances would not violate natural justice because the parties had been heard.

rule.if: public_interest_writ and mining_lease_in_forest_land and renewal_enabled_by_court_order and not prior_central_approval_obtained

predicates.public_interest_writ: The proceeding is a public-interest writ concerning environmental protection and mining.
predicates.mining_lease_in_forest_land: The mining lease concerns land that is forest land.
predicates.renewal_enabled_by_court_order: A court order or decree enabled mining to continue after a lease expired or enabled the lease to be renewed.
predicates.prior_central_approval_obtained: The required prior approval of the Central Government has been obtained for the non-forest use of the land.

issues.definition: A court order enabling renewal or continued mining in forest land must be set aside when the required prior approval was not obtained.

issues.legal_issue: A mine operating under an unexpired original lease may be permitted to continue until that lease expires, subject to legal and environmental safeguards, but is not entitled to renewal.
material_facts: Three mines were operating under valid original leases whose terms had not yet expired.
The Court considered their ongoing operation, the investments involved, employment effects, and the need to phase out mining.
The Court imposed environmental safeguards, required undertakings, and authorized monitoring; it also directed that the leases could not be renewed.
issues.conclusion: The three ongoing mines could continue until expiry of their original leases, subject to the specified legal requirements and environmental safeguards, after which mining had to stop and no renewal application could be entertained.
issues.legal_principle: The Court balanced environmental protection and forest conservation against the practical effects of immediate closure. The permission was a transitional measure for mines already operating under unexpired original leases, not a right to renewal; the forest-conservation requirements remained applicable.

rule.if: public_interest_writ and mine_currently_operating and original_lease_unexpired and environmental_safeguards_are_imposed

predicates.public_interest_writ: The proceeding is a public-interest writ addressing environmental harm from mining.
predicates.mine_currently_operating: The mine is operating when the Court considers whether it may continue.
predicates.original_lease_unexpired: The mine’s original lease term has not expired.
predicates.environmental_safeguards_are_imposed: The Court requires conditions intended to protect the environment and ecological balance during continued operation.

issues.definition: An operating mine with an unexpired original lease may continue only to the end of that lease term when the Court imposes environmental safeguards.

issues.legal_issue: A mine that has already stopped operating cannot be reopened merely to give its owner treatment equal to that of a mine still operating, subject to a narrowly supported exception.
material_facts: Several mines with valid leases were not operating when the Court considered whether they could reopen.
The Court had decided that mining in the area should be phased out and declined to allow fresh mining operations at mines that had stopped.
One small-area mine outside forest and municipal areas was treated as a special case after its owner undertook not to mine adjoining private land and to restore vegetation and forest growth.
issues.conclusion: The non-operating mines were not permitted to reopen merely to equalize treatment, but the specially supported mine could operate until its lease expired subject to the undertaking and monitoring.
issues.legal_principle: In the interests of the community, the Court could treat operating and non-operating mines differently during the transition to closure. Equal treatment did not require reopening mines already stopped; the Court made a limited exception based on the particular site and a concrete restoration undertaking.

rule.if: public_interest_writ and general_mining_closure_order and mine_not_operating and not exceptional_site_and_reclamation_commitment

predicates.public_interest_writ: The proceeding is a public-interest writ concerning environmental harm from mining.
predicates.general_mining_closure_order: The Court has determined that mining in the area must be phased out or stopped.
predicates.mine_not_operating: The mine has already stopped operating when reopening is considered.
predicates.exceptional_site_and_reclamation_commitm: The mine has a sufficiently distinct site and its owner has given a specific commitment to restore vegetation and avoid mining on adjoining land.

issues.definition: A mine that has stopped operating cannot reopen under a general closure order unless its site and restoration commitment support a special exception.

issues.legal_issue: Displaced mine owners affected by closure in the public interest should have a structured process for pursuing alternative occupation or rehabilitation.
material_facts: The Court’s closure directions displaced mine owners and ended their mining operations without compensation.
The record did not show that the governments had made adequate alternative arrangements for the displaced owners.
The Court considered that rehabilitation required a time-bound and coordinated process involving relevant governments and experts.
issues.conclusion: A committee was to be constituted to oversee the rehabilitation of displaced mine owners and consider alternative mining sites while taking ecological and environmental concerns into account.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that closure in the broad interests of the community did not eliminate the need to provide displaced mine owners with alternative occupation. An effective rehabilitation direction required a functioning, coordinated process rather than a merely general observation.

predicates.public_interest_writ: The proceeding is a public-interest case in which the Court orders closure for the community’s benefit.
predicates.mine_owners_displaced_by_closure: Mine owners lose their mining activity as a result of the Court’s closure directions.
predicates.no_effective_rehabilitation_arrangement: The record does not show an effective arrangement for alternative occupation or rehabilitation.

issues.definition: When a public-interest closure displaces mine owners and no effective alternative arrangement exists, a rehabilitation process is required.

issues.legal_issue: A monitoring body may be established to supervise environmental restoration and the limited mining allowed during a transition to closure.
material_facts: The Court ordered the closure of mining generally but permitted limited continued operation of three mines under conditions.
The area required reafforestation, restoration of water flows, and supervision of mining safeguards.
The existing governmental reafforestation programme had not shown sufficient improvement, and the Court considered continuing oversight necessary.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed the constitution of a monitoring committee to oversee reafforestation, mining safeguards, and other measures needed to restore normal environmental conditions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court used its authority in the public-interest proceeding to ensure that its closure, restoration, and limited-operation directions were implemented and monitored.

predicates.public_interest_writ: The proceeding is a public-interest case concerning environmental protection.
predicates.environmental_restoration_needed: The area requires reafforestation or other measures to restore environmental conditions.
predicates.limited_mining_continues_under_court_con: Some mining is temporarily permitted subject to conditions imposed by the Court.

issues.definition: When environmental restoration is needed and mining temporarily continues under court-imposed conditions, an environmental monitoring body is required.
